newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African leader misses summit due to mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Central African leader misses summit due to mutiny.

text.p: An army mutiny that has paralysed the Central African Republic forced President Ange-Felix Patasse to miss a Franco-African summit on Wednesday, his spokesman said.
A meeting between Patasse and former President Andre Kolingba, to whom mutineers are believed to owe allegiance, has so far failed to defuse the two-week-old mutiny.

Residents said Bangui remained divided between a rebel-held south and west and a northern sector controlled by loyalist forces backed by French troops based in the former French colony under bilateral accords. Sporadic firing could be heard.
The split is along tribal lines and residents fearing clashes have been leaving districts dominated by rival ethnic groups for other parts of the capital or home provinces.
Presidential spokesman Prosper Douba said the mutiny had forced Patasse to miss a summit in the Burkina Fasso capital Ouagadougou of France and its former African colonies.
"As a result of the situation in Bangui, President Patasse can no longer go to Ouagadougou," Douba told Gabon-based Africa No 1 radio on Tuesday night.

He said Patasse, whose resignation is demanded by mutineers for allegedly arming civilian militias, expected "heads of state of friendly countries to send delegations and commissions of inquiry" to Bangui to assess the situation.
"As you know, a democratically elected president is prevented from exercising power. That is absolutely intolerable," Douba said.

"So, we are expecting the summit to examine the situation and the heads of state to make a decision on it and condemn what is going on, because we know that the rebels benefit from the support of a number of friendly forces who supply them with arms and ammunition," Douba said in the report monitored by the BBC.
Kolingba, who met Patasse during crisis talks involving the country's 23 political parties, said later he would work with the president to defuse the crisis.
The former president was defeated by Patasse in elections in 1993. He is from the Yakoma tribe like most of the rebel soldiers but denies fomenting the revolt.
The mutiny, the country's third this year, has shifted from grievances over pay and status to a bid to oust Patasse.
Rebels reiterated on Tuesday they would not return to barracks until they had disarmed civilians and African mercenaries from Chad and Sudan backing the president.
At least seven people have been killed since the rebellion started on November 16, according to hospital sources.
Witnesses said barricades mounted by members of Patasse's Baya tribe went up in the Combatants area and Sarra. Militants looking for Yakomas checked residents' identities.
Roadblocks also appeared on roads into rebel strongholds.
French troops who helped put down a more serious mutiny in May are protecting Patasse and key points in the city but have not clashed with rebels.
